blocks.x: For me, my name is Albert Warner. Albert Warner. Albert Warner. Albert Warner. Any middle name?

No, any middle name. Born in New Orleans, Louisiana. December 31st, 1890. When I first started learning music was with a half brother of mine. He learned from Henri Dutre. Well when he left, before he left he bought him a new trombone. And a boy wanted to buy his old trombone from him. And he refused to sell it to him. He paid one against his brother. Well, he sent downtown, got me, and I went on up to his house to see what it was all about. I got there, he gave me this little old brass horn with about a bell the size of a saucer. A little chatois, a little French horn. Well, and I told him, I didn't have time to be aware of that thing. So he said, well, you got the line. He said, I'm getting ready to leave, New Orleans. He says, and I want you to take and learn this thing. I said, oh, I don't have time with that. Well, what he did, he went and put it together. He handed it to me. He said, well, blow on it. Well, when I first picked it up, I couldn't blow it. So he said, well, keep on. I just took the thing, kept it blowing in the first position. So finally, I made a note in there. I said, what note is that? He said, well, that's B flat. So he said, keep on blowing. So after I made that note, I said, well, he pushed it in the second position. He held my hand and showed me the second position. Well, I made that note. Well, then he turned around and shoved my hand in the third position. I made that note. Well, after that, that kind of made me kind of like the thing. I said, well, chefs, this thing ain't as hard as I thought it was. So finally, before I left there, he had me making those three positions. He said, now, well, what I want you to do now, he says, go down and buy your method. He says, and come up here twice a week. He says, I'm going to give you this. I don't know. Well, about 22. And...
Had you played anything before that at all, like drums or guitar or anything?

No, never worried about music. I had the opportunity to learn to play piano, but I was a fast man at the time. Didn't have time to worry about music. So after that, I went and bought the method and started going up there twice a week. So finally, I got the first, second and third position. Learned how to make those notes in the end. And so after he left, I went with Steve. Well, Steve, well, he wasn't a great musician. Well, I went on to him and taken a couple of lessons with him. Did he play? He played a trombone tune. Steve? Yeah, Steve. What was his last name? What was Steve's last name, Sonny? Arthur. Arthur Steve? Yeah. Yeah. That's his first name, Arthur, huh? Yeah, Arthur. Yeah, Arthur Steve. He lived right around Houston, Phillips Street.
He's still living, huh?

No, he's dead now. Yeah. He's still living, huh? And so I've taken a couple of lessons with him. So finally, Giles was putting up a band, Clay Giles' brother. Well, after I learned, before that, I got a self-instructor. A fellow sent off to New York and got me a self-instructor. Well, I went on and I started practicing out to self-instructor. So at the time, I was in the pressing business, too, and still working where I'm at, where I just retired from.
Telegram.

Yeah. And so every time I'd blow the horn, I'd lay it down. I'd go press a piece. I'd come back, blow the horn, go back and press another piece. And my wife says, gee whiz, you make me sick with this thing. I said, well, I might make you sick now. I said, but someday this thing will come in handy. Because I'd find out what it was all about, you see. So finally, after I kind of got good with it, Giles came along. He wanted me to join a little band that was putting up a little brass band back on that street. So I went on with the brass band. And so they call it the Bulls Band. So I used to rehearse with them every Sunday. So this same boy, what he was talking about, Pete, what we call him, being the Pete Picker. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And I used to go by Pete. And Pete used to help me out a whole lot, you know. And he'd show me a different thing because he used to come around the band, too.
Well, what part of town were you born? Did you give that street?

Well, right around St. Ann and Roman. You lived around that part most of your life? I brought up around this neighborhood. Right around what they call the Tramie, you see. I brought up around this neighborhood, yeah. And so bring back this.
Pete, you were talking about.

With Pete there, so we'd go to the barbershop on Bienville Street there. We'd rehearse a lot in there, him and I, just the bass and the trombone. So this fellow, Amos White. That's right. Amos White would come along, and he'd join in with us. And he would write off a little piece of music there and make me go over that music, you know. And so finally, I got pretty good with it. So this little band formed up. I went with them. They called it the Bulls Band. So I went on and started playing with them. So the first job they had for Carnival Day, Steve said, well, I wasn't good enough. He wouldn't take me out. So the boy said, well, he says, you better take him, would you? He said, you'll have some kind of help. So he went on out there, and then he come out there. He fell down on the job. You see? The next job they got was down at the Holy Ghost Church, a Holy Redeemer down on Royal and Luson Field. So I went on down there, and I played this job with him, and went back in the woods here somewhere. They were short of a trumpet player, and they pick up a trumpet player back there. So this fellow walked up to me. He says, where are you from? I said, I'm from New Orleans. He said, I never seen you before. I said, no. I said, first time I was out. He said, well, you say, first time you was out? He said, I don't understand. He says, you playing as good as this fellow? Yeah. This is an old musician. I said, well, I said, that's my teacher. He said, you're a teacher? He said, you done beat your teacher. I said, yeah? He said, yeah, you done beat your teacher. So after that, I just went from band to band after I got good, and I started playing with the college fellow, what you was calling there? Louis Demene and Eddie Jackson. So they sent downtown and got me. They were living uptown, so they said they wanted me to play with them. So I went on and started playing in a little band they had up there.
No name to it, just the?

Just Louis Demene and Eddie Jackson. That's the role. So I went on to playing with them. So after I left them, I went with a fellow by the name of William, the Columbia Band. See, and after I left the Columbia Band, and I went on, I went to the Camellia Band. Well, the Camellia had a pretty good pull around this town here. They had work in the countries and down Violet and all those different places, Bertrandville. They was doing pretty good work.
Who was the leader?
Joe Nicholas. Remember Joe Nicholas? Oh, sure, yeah. Yeah, he was with them then. Oh, Lord, then. Him and Louis Cabot. Well, that's not bad, huh?
Why you call it that?

I went playing along with them, so I went with Chris Kelly and different fellas, you know, I would go around playing with. Okay, that's good. So the next band I got with was Kid Rene. Well, I stayed with Kid Rene a good while. And I was-
And was that a brass band or the dance band?

No, dance band. Yeah, yeah. And I'd leave him. And when I left him, I went with another fella had a band around there. Well, I stayed with him for a pretty good while until it got around depression time. When it got around depression, I just gave up playing. Yeah. Stopped altogether.
I was going to ask some more about some of the names you mentioned. Eddie Jackson on tuba. Eddie Jackson on tuba. People tell me he was pretty good. Was he really that good?
It was the best they had.

That's right. It was the best they had. Because we were just too few. Yeah, because you see him, you could be 15 blocks off, and if Eddie blow the horn, you could say, blow that tuba, you could say, that's Eddie Jackson coming from you. That's right.
Oh, somebody was telling a big professor on that the other day. He was talking about how he used to blow down a fence now and then. Is that really good?
Oh, no. You see, Eddie Jackson. It was a fist. It was a fist.
Eddie Jackson blow it. He had a different tone than anybody else. And you could tell any piece he played, you could tell it was him playing it, because he played it different than anybody else.
Yes, sir. Did he do a lot of more notes or faster fingering or just louder? What was he so good at?
It's just a tonation that he had in that horn. I don't know. The other fellas looked like they just didn't have it.
Listen, in other words, he could go up and get a note, regardless how it is, and then drop down. Drop down there and come down. A lot of range.
See, like I said, come right on down with that note. Like these fellas, there's a number of, there plays around here. We play it all the time.
Killman puts in a thing like that sometimes. Lead and Savvy?
Yeah. I heard nobody else play that thing since Eddie died. That's right.
Well, those breaks that John plays on clarinet, you know.
That's for the bass to play.
Yeah.
I want to get that straight. That's for the bass. That's right.
And who would be good on that? Eddie Jackson and who else? Anybody?
Eddie Jackson's about the only one I ever heard made that thing.
He made it right.
But of course, Porter could do it. Yeah, Porter.
Yeah, John Porter.

Yeah, John Porter. John Porter, yeah. Who was this guy, Basie, by the way? Huh? Basie. Oh, Lil Basie. Lil Basie was good, too. The little kid went, you know, little bit of kid went to California by that day?
Oh, yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah. He was good on it, too. Yeah, yeah. He was pretty good on it, too. That's right. Yeah, Lil Basie. Yeah. He went to California.
What's his right name? Did you know?
I know his family's good. They used to live right at the corner from us, sonny. Yeah. Right at Orleans and Roman. Yeah. Mitchell.
Mitchell. Basie Mitchell, huh?
Yeah.
I never heard of him. Did you meet him out in California?
Yeah, he's a little bit of short fella, just about that big. Did he play trumpet or anything else? No, he played straight, straight, upright bass and bass violin. Yeah. Yeah.
Los Angeles or San Francisco, do you think? You'll find him someday.
Let's see. I believe he's in Los Angeles.
We'll ask Sidney Dazvines. Is he about the same age as you, Mr. Warner, or is he younger?
Oh, he's young. He's younger than us. Young than us. Yeah, he's younger than us. Yeah. Yeah, he's younger than us. He's, uh... He was a kid when he was around...
Around the years.
That's old man Mitchell's son.
Yeah, his brother lives... Where is he? Yeah. His brother lives here? Yeah.
Well, his brother can tell exactly where he's at. Where's his brother on... On Valera, right?
No, but he is... Yeah, he's that way. He even got me to see.
Oh, catch him. Well, he can find out what part of California he's in. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, when you first learned on your trombone, did you learn to read right away out of that method?

Start right... Right and learn how to read, because I couldn't play a thing out of head. Yeah. See? And whenever anybody contradict me, say I wasn't making something right, I went to this man here. See? Him and I got in the room together, he said, well, go on over it. So I'd go on over to a piece of music, and say, there's nothing wrong with it. I said, well, they tell me I'm wrong. He said, you're not wrong. I said, that's why I brought it to you, see if I'm wrong. I said, if you say it's right, it must be right then. I go back to the fellas, I said, well, you all can play the way you want.
What about Kid René's dance band? Now, did he play by ear or by music?

They played music and by air too, but they was better on this routine stuff than they was on music. See? Because a lot of time they had music up there, they just was guessing at it. Especially the psyche.
The band was in that band at that time.
Well, the time I was playing at them, they had Kid René, Edna Mitchell, Joe René, myself, Manny Gabriel. What's this boy, what you say, boy, he put up there with you all?
Andy.
Andy. Andy. Henry Harden. Where did Henry Harden play? Henry Harden. Henry Harden played the saxophone. But he wouldn't play alto. No, he played the baritone.
Did Hamdi play clarinet tune?
No, he played saxophone.
He played alto too.
And they had another boy from Bay St. Louis there. His dad is a musician, Bay St. Louis.
What instrument? Did he play saxophone?
He played sax. Yeah. And they had this other boy playing bass. What his name there? Lazard? Chester Lazard. Chester Lazard, yeah. Chester Lazard. He was playing bass.
That was a pretty big band, that wasn't it?
Ten pieces.
Ten pieces. Ten piece band. Two trumpets or one?

They had, let's see, they had Rene, they had Rene and myself, Edna Mitchell, Joe Rene, Chester Lazard, and Henry Harden, Thomas on guitar, and they had Manny Gabriel, Handy, and this boy over the river, from over the lake, ten pieces.
Who was Thomas on guitar? What was his name?
Remember Thomas? He lived on Sedan and Claiborne. Remember he used to play banjo?
Yeah, Thomas did that.
Yeah. That's all I ever know about Thomas.
Was he related to Tom Benton?
No, his last name was Thomas. Oh, I see. Yeah, his last name was Thomas.
Who was in some of the other bands you played? What's more about that Rene band? Was that before the Depression? About when was that?
Well, that's just a little before Depression. They was playing upon their story.
In the 1920s up there?
Yeah, around about 27, 28. Because we played up there, it must have been about a year and a half.
Was that before Lee Collins and Rogashow and a bunch went in there?

Or was it after that? Lee Collins used to come up there. Well, you see, after they left from up there, then they started playing what you call percentage jobs. Then they was using different bands. See? Then Lee Collins left here and he went on up to Chicago, I believe. New York, some of those places.
Somebody called that the Astoria Roof. Was it sort of a roof garden? Did they call it that?
Well, they used to call it a roof garden, but it was the same as a dance hall, you see.
It was all closed in.
All closed in, yeah.
Davey Jones was in there after you or before you?

Oh, he must have got in there after us. Mm-hmm. Yeah, after us. You see, because after I left Rene, I went playing with some other fellas there. Some little scrap band they had. I don't remember what band it was. Then right after I left, well then that's where Beansy was running the place, well then he cut them down. They went to playing percentage, you see, and that's where Rene left, you see.
Mm-hmm.

Then Remy had a band. He used to come up there, you see. Is that T-Boy? T-Boy Remy. He used to come up there and play it too. Mm-hmm. He used to use different bands up there after we left. Yeah, different bands he used.
He's in California too, man. Yeah, he's in California. He'll get out there again sometime. See all the fellas.
I guess I'll be up there pretty soon. Not to stay there.
You were just going out for a visit.
Yeah, I got my son up there. The saxophone player? Mm-hmm.
Oh, what was your half-brother's name? I didn't get that.
Euless Jackson.
Well, I've heard of him.
Oh, he's dead. He died in Chicago.
Who did he play with?
Well, he used to play with the Excelsior Band. That was years ago, you see. Then he left. He didn't stay up very long after that.
Mm-hmm.
Then he left and he went to Chicago. He played with Honoré Dutré.
Mm-hmm.
You remember when Honoré was playing with Excelsior? Dutré, Trumont player? Yeah. Sure. You remember that big fella? Big babysit, but look like a type. Yeah. That's who I'm speaking of.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah.
What's up with guns? You're annoying.
Because Honoré Lloyd-Tem, you see. Yeah, I understand. Well, after Honoré Lloyd-Tem, he said, well, he says, you see the Albert Lloyd-Nard play.
He was a good one to it.
Yeah. Good musician he was.
Who else in your family played?
Well, I ain't got just my son, the one that's in California. That's the only one that played. My daddy, he played bass, but that was way before Sonny's time.
What kind of bass did he play? Bass viola. I mean, in the dance band? Yeah, dance band, yeah. The string bass.
The string bass, yeah.
He played with the bass, I believe.

Yeah, but he might have played with the bass. That's before your time and my time. Yeah, sure. I just wondered who he played. Yeah. In any particular band, you remember? No, no particular band that I know of.
Yeah.
I guess he played with some of these old musicians like himself, because right now if he was living, he'd be about 90 years old.
A scrap band, you see, and he'd just pick up and say, come on, let's go have a little fun. I guess that's the kind of band he was in at that time, you see.

Yeah, those fellas used to have, back in that time, they had a lot of old musicians, you know, like Jimmy Brown, that fella's name, used to play there. Jimmy Brown, another dude they used to play over here at the cooperators hall. I can't think of his name. What'd you see at that time? It was, it was all, oh, you wasn't, you wasn't in the city then.
You remember Billy Marrero? Lawrence Marrero's father?
No, I don't remember him well.
You, you, you don't remember? You don't remember the superior band?
I remember the superior, but I don't know Marrero's daddy. I know his brothers. You see, I know all the boys, but I don't know, I don't know the old man.
You heard it, you heard him, I guess, and didn't know him. I didn't know him, you see. Because I'm, he was, had the superior. Yeah. It was really his band.
Yeah, I remember, like, they had, back in that time, they had the superior and some other old band there. They had a lot of old bands.
Remember the Olympia band? The Olympia. Or the Kemperd or anybody around here? You remember hearing Kemperd when you were a kid?
Oh, yeah.
Tell them about what they used to call you. You remember we were talking about how people get your name confused?

Oh, yeah. Well, you see, Kemperd was kind of a little cousin of mine, you know. Well, they used to call me Freddy Kemperd. Oh, really? Yeah. His brother, Louis, lives around on Burry Street now, you see. And they say, well, that's my cousin. You see, well, they called him, called me Freddy Kemperd. Everywhere I went, people used to call me Freddy Kemperd.
Did you look like him some, too?
Well, I looked just that much.
He looked that awfully heavy before he died. I never saw him.
Yeah, well. You see, when Freddy started, he started off on the violin. See? Yeah. Up beyond Burry and St. Louis. He was nothing but a little kid then. And from that he took up a cornet.
What was happening around Burry and St. Louis? Was it a ballroom or one of those?
Well, Burry and St. Louis. Well, no, there was houses like. I mean, one part they had a bakery at the corner. They had a grocery and bar. And that other part, they had a barroom there.
Yeah.
On the riverside. Yeah. Yeah.
And would he play in the ballroom or would he just stand outside?

Well, he played, you know, he used to play at home, but after he learned, you know, and he started playing all them different little tunks around him, you know, then he left and he went away. See? Yeah. He left here and went on to Chicago. I believe he left before Oliver did.
Does that make sense?
Yeah. I believe he left before Oliver left here.
Did you hear, remember Oliver playing here?

Oh, yeah. I used to go dance for Oliver's music. He used to play around here at the Economy Hall. Yeah, I used to be at him and, was that the fellow here in California now? Kid Ori? Ori? Yeah. That's when Oliver left here. I was at the last dance he played over at the Economy Hall.
How did Ori play? Was he a head man or read much or pretty rough or a nice tone?

Well, he had a nice tone in his trombone. To me, he did back in that time as far as, you know, as I had an understanding. I used to like his playing, because everywhere he was playing I would be there. I heard him. But I didn't have no interest in no music then, you see, back in those days.

I heard him a couple of times, but I think he's most of his man. Yeah. Of course he can play. You see, Jim, him and Jim is all in the same style. Anytime he said, I mean, they're going to play it. They're going to play it naturally too. But I think he's most of his...

Well, what is he, a real teen? Yeah. You see, that's the thing I didn't know. I'm telling you, right back in those days, I didn't know. All I'd know, I used to just go to the dancers, they could sit down there and play it. I wouldn't know if he was playing my head or not.

I know as a little guy, but not too much, I understand. But I know that he wasn't a man on my top or Hashton Bond, you understand? Or Lewis Nelson, he wasn't on the top of them. Oh, yes. But he was a good man, you understand? Just like Jim. Now, what did he do, what did he call me? Jim. He said, hello, Mr. Jim. I said, hello. But my name is not Jim. But I used to say, Jim. I said, okay. I said, how you feeling? Okay. Because he said, I'm Jim. He said, brother, of course, we kind of feel with him. And when we talk, we almost talk like that. But he's no kid at all.
You taught him drum on and taught him how to talk too?

No, no. I don't know. Wait, wait, wait a minute. It looks that way. Wait, wait, wait a minute. Goddamn. I couldn't talk once. I couldn't talk once. I had a much. How can I teach when I taught? I couldn't talk once. But, let me tell you, kid. He said, sometime, when he and I get together, I said, I said, I said, partner? I said, I said, I'm learning how to talk good. He gave me a lesson. He said, I'll find him out sometime, you see. Well, they did tell me that Sonny was Jim's uncle.
I'm the teacher. Jim's uncle though. No.

Uncle? No, we used to know him. You did know him, of course, down in the country. Yeah, I know him so long. I know him, I understand, first. I didn't know him. I think he's teacher. But sometimes he would get to talk. I said, partner, I said, you are learning good how to talk. I said, just keep on using it.

You see, getting back now to that Eureka band there. Oh, yeah. See, way back, say, about as far as I can remember, Connish had come to get me to play with the Eureka band. Well, Connish, he was no kind of reader, which Sonny knew that. But he always wanted somebody that, you know, would help him out. So he come and he got me to play one job. After he got me to play one job, well he did just like I did Sonny. Well then he say, you stay here. I said, all right, so I'll continue playing with him. So after I got to making a lot of jobs out in the country, the band was kind of going down, they wasn't doing much work. I started going to country and playing and Wilson was running a little candy stand and he didn't have time to be worried. So I said, well you run your candy stand, I'm going to play music. So when they'd get something they didn't want me to play, I told them, I'm going to country. So he said, well I have to get somebody to play. So I said, all right, you get somebody to play. I said, well get Red. He said, Red play trombone. So that's how he got Red in the band. He played with it, yeah. You were in the band before Red. I was in the band before Red, you see. Do you remember his father?
His father had been... Well I don't know his father.
Don't remember him. No, I don't know anything about his father.
He's been one of the organizers of a real old band.
Well see me, I'm the only old man in there, I mean from old back. I'm the only old man in there. When did you join it?
Do you remember about that year?
I wouldn't know exactly what year it was.
Before the Depression, the time you were with Kid Renee or after that?

No, that was after Depression. Let's see this. There it was around about... See Depression in 29. Must have been around about... 20... 37... 38... Something around about that. Yeah. Or it might have been before that, you see. Yeah, a little bit. Long before that. But I'm just giving a rough guess at it, you know. Yeah. About around about that time, you see. Well at that time we used to rehearsal up and down Ramport Street. See, sometimes they rehearsaled in the back of one ballroom. And then next time they rehearsaled in the back of a restroom. See, they didn't have no regular place. You remember the time Lewis came down here to play that peanut vendor? Yeah. Well that's the time I was playing with them then. Well that was around what... It was around about 19... In the 30s anyway.
Was that when Lewis was at the suburban gardens?
Yeah. What year was that?
That was way back, 1931 then. Yeah.
Yeah, around about that time. About the time Buddy Petit died, do you remember? Yeah, when Buddy Petit died. It's because we played Buddy Petit's funeral, you see.
What, you were in the Eureka when you played Buddy Petit's funeral?

I was in the Eureka, I was in the Eureka's but I went and played with Rene to play Buddy's funeral, you see. But for the Lewis, when Lewis came in, we went and picked up Lewis up at the L&A depot there. Oh I see. And that peanut vendor was out then. That time they was playing the peanut vendor. They had people around there like that. They didn't know what was coming up until they seen him getting off the train then. We brought him through Canal Street there.
Whose band were you playing with then?
Eureka's. Eureka's at that time. Already then. Yeah, it had to be the Eureka's because that was the Zulus band then, you see.
I wonder if they had all brass bands or some dance bands running down there. I heard there were several bands down there to meet or something.
They had one brass band and if I'm not mistaken they had one band in a wagon like, you know, playing on the furniture wagon there.
I thought maybe Kid Rene or somebody was there at that time, there in a wagon.

I don't remember what band it was that was in the wagon but I know we was the marching band, you see. And because we played, we played on Troupe Canal Street. We brought him on up to the hotel there. He was staying at that hotel on Julian Ramport. What did you call it? The Patterson? The Patterson Hotel, yeah. The Patterson Hotel, yeah.
Had you just joined the Eureka then or had you been with them a while?
Well, I hadn't been with them very long then. I guess about that time, yeah.
Who else was in the Eureka then when you joined?

Well, at that time there was Willie Wilson, Johnny Wilson, myself, Connish, Flowers, Flowers. Let's see who they had on the bass drum. I think Lil' Jimmy was playing. What the other? Groundhog? Yeah, Groundhog. Groundhog? Yeah.
Yeah, that's what you mean.
They had to use a card. They had another fellow on snare drum, I can't think of his name.
Was that Jim Mewkes? Is that the name?
And they had, if I'm not mistaken, George Lewis was playing a card. Black Benny's buddy, huh?
Yeah, yeah. George Lewis.
Yeah, I believe George Lewis was playing a clarinet.
When did Schatz play with the Eureka?
Schatz, yeah, Schatz was playing. Way back then in the week. Schatz was playing too. There was three trumpets, Schatz, Willie Wilson, and they had some other fellow playing with Willie Wilson.
When did Landry come to town?

No, Landry, let's see. No, I believe, yeah, Landry was with him. Yeah, Landry was with him because I used to kid, Landry, begging a cigarette. That's how I do that. Lick his fingers. He meant for somebody to give him a cigarette, you see. Yeah. That's what we used to get a kick out of it. So when I first saw him do that, I didn't know what he was talking about. Then the fellow would say he's begging for cigarettes. Yeah, he would be begging for cigarettes. That was their lineup. Landry, Schatz, and Willie Wilson. Johnny Wilson on baritone, and Verrett on tuba. You remember that? Yeah, I remember him. Connish and I, and Flowers on that alto, and they had them two drums. Let's see, they had a clarinet. I'm sure if it was George Lewis. Does Flowers still live around here, or did he move down? He runs on the base. I mean he runs on the ship. He lives down my way somewhere. I saw him a week before, let's see, Christmas week.
He lived down my way.
I knew his address too, you know. He used to live around here, I know, didn't he? Yeah, he used to live around Verrett Street, Verrett Domain.

Not far from here. Yeah, but he moved down below, cause I see his wife sometime around St. Bernard Street. Yeah. But he was running on the ship all the time. Well the ship, yeah. He was mostly on the ship. He don't play anymore at all. No, he don't play anymore at all. No, he don't play anymore at all. Don't go on, that's too bad.
There's no alto players and no-
What boy, that ain't no joke. And no baritones.
No baritones, you see that's what's missing in those bands, those baritones, those alto, those melophones, those French halls we used to call them.
Was there any saxes in the Eureka band when you joined?
Well no, they had a clarinet and that peck horn, that melophone.
The baritone horn and all that.

Yeah, and the baritone horn. Johnny Wilson was playing baritone. Yeah. Just after that, after the band started getting scattered out, they started putting clarinet, I mean saxophone and baritone horn like they got now. Cutting out the other. Cutting out all that, you see.
The brass and the instruments, and that's the main thing that they should have. Peg horn in the band.

That peg horn and that baritone is missing. Yeah. Because they got some of that, we got some of that old music up there now, if Red was to go through it. I'll show you that old music we used to play. I was showing Sonny a piece there at, what you call it, the Chicago Tribune. The Tribune, yeah.
The Chicago Tribune. Right over there.
We got all that there. Red's got a lot of old music that we used to use up there. See?

Yeah, I saw some of that. All good music too. He's ready though, because at bass, we got to work there. And then he's no doggone well. If he come here with me, I'm going to be on him with that bass part because he's no active bass part. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
The bass parts are tough on some of those things.

Yeah, tough. You see those bass parts there, some of these fellas are not fast enough with these fingers. See them fingers, they got their fingers too stiff on it. Your fingers got to be super, just the same as theirs on the trumpet. But you can't press down on that thing like this. No, it's heavy, yeah. Your fingers got to be super. Now you're the man who can handle one of those. He can handle the bass.

But I'm going to put him on the bass, you see? Now you see the irony of this. With your bass, you've got to know the artificial thing, you understand? So if something comes difficult to you, you must know how to make one thing one way. You must know how to steal and do everything. You must take advantage of your instrument. Never let the instrument take advantage of you. And so then that's where I feel at all times, you see? The thing that I see is easy to make, that's the way I make it. The same way with the trombone, you see? Well, that's what I'm talking about. You see, there's just things that you can make on the trombone. You can make an artificial note.
That's the idea. Make an artificial note, you see? That's true. Use that third valve sometimes and catch funny things, you know?
No, no, no. You're right.
No, no, no. That's the third valve. And sometimes that first and third valve, it gets a lot of things too.

Yeah, but if you don't know it, how are you going to do it? That's right. If you don't know it, you can't make it, there you are. You just got to be guessing. That's all. Because even while you're guessing, the band's gone. That's right.

Look, don't be afraid what you're going to say. We can save these tapes and not play them for anybody. I say this is for a hundred years from now. You know, if you want to, we can put like a restriction on it, they call it, you know? And not to be played for ten years, you know, or something. So don't worry, just speak your mind.
Sure.
You know what I mean?
That's all you can do. You don't think you have to know. You see, Jim, just like you always say about Jim. Jim, he's my friend. Yeah, we all know that.
We know your buddies, yeah.

Yeah, but they all, sometimes some guy, oh, did Jim beat you? I say, yeah. Yeah, Jim, did Jim know more than you? I say, yeah. I don't tell him. I say, good. I say, but one thing, I say, Jim, he makes a living more of this than I have. I have made my living more of this too. I say, well, what do you use me, knock in the gym? You understand? When? I've come along. I did good. He might come up. But, and then this is the question I asked him. I said, sir, if a man go to school, I said, understand me very well. You don't go to school. I said, if a newspaper, if I can take a newspaper and read it and you can't read it, I said, who is the most best man? The question has not been answered yet with me, with the first words to me. Oh, he can do it and you can do it and you can do it and you can do it and you can do it. But I said, answer my question. As yet, it has not been answered as yet.
In other words, if he get a check, he put a cross mark and you can sign your name, well there's a big difference in it.
Well, and then he signed it.

You see, he's all right in his style of things. He can play it. You can play with fellas that can use you in those things. Me too. I like his playing. You go get with some other bands like Up The Line, now you know when you go up the line that routine's all right but they want you to see too. You can only say, I'm a trombone player, you see, and I can play. All right. Now when you say you can play they're going to get that music, they're going to put it there. All right. You're going to wait until somebody started playing? Well that man ain't waiting until somebody else started playing, he won't see what you're doing. And you can't fool them people. You see it all the time. We get up and you read that musician, this book there. They sometimes call for men. They want a man that can fake and read too. You've got to do both. Well how the hell are they going to do it? If you can fake and you can't read, well they can't use you. You can get out and play with these fellas that know that you can fake, well then they're going to let you go by with that. See? But if they ever get any place where they've got to, all of them do some reading themselves, well then that's where you at. Tornpee then. You're handicapped. You're just like a crippled child. But I'm going to tell you about Jim.

I just wish that I could play with him in a way of speaking, you understand? Of course I know that I'm his superior, you understand? But when I'm speaking, but he started playing, you understand? And Jim, if you ever get in there one time, boy, he's going to make you sick. But that man don't forget nothing though. No, we got a lot of life to it. I want to tell you, you can say what you want, I don't care what nobody says, Jim is a good, tailgate man. That's right. Me, I've tried my whole life to try and make him learn how to read like I could. But if Jim had learned the way I learned, Jim would be one of the best trombone players in the city.

I wonder, did Jim learn to read a little bit? He told me once he could read some, but I thought maybe his eyes, you know, his eyes aren't too good for reading without glasses. I thought maybe that was part of it.
No, he's damn hit.
He still couldn't read even with glasses. This man tried his damnedest to learn him out of reading.

That's to say. I wondered whether he really wanted to or not. No, this is the truth. I'm not telling you a lot. He ain't right. But I'm not telling you, that's what I'm going to play. I'll tell the world, any time you jump on Jim, you're going to jump on the man. With his band and putting the team in there. But no, of course, if he's going to come out with your record. No, it's a different attitude. You change your living. If you know, you're in a hell of a place.

Just like he said, he says, if Sonny is there or I'm there, he don't mind filling in for either one of us. Yeah, I've heard him get along pretty well. He said if either one of us ain't there, he said he don't want to play.

Because it's the side there. You see, I don't want against nobody. He'll fuck me up out there. You understand? That's the right. But now if a guy want to come in and see what he can do, this thing, you know, I'm going to try and do it. When a party gets in the party now, I'm going to take my whole line. I'm going to see what he's going to do. But if a person comes out, you understand? Be nice, but I'm sure I'm going to have him work. And then again, my band, I'm going to let my band fall for trying to take revenge or someone else. No, I wouldn't do that. And if I see he's kind of weak and coming to some place, if I know he's weak for that, I'm coming in there. And that's my band. I don't want my band to go down just because a guy come in and see what he can do it. And then when he gets there, he can't do it. But that don't make sense for me. Then I know, I'm going to let my band go down, I wouldn't do it. I'm coming on in there. It's my old band and that's what we do.

You see, like him and I, we're about the only two that I know of yet. That's it. You see, now like, like sometimes you might see me look over at him. Well, that means that I'm going down, you see. But if I throw my horn up, he know I'm going to pick up. And if I put my, lay my horn down like this, he know that I'm going to pull down. If he do the same thing, I know he's going to take down, you see. And if he put his horn up, I know he's going to go up. So that's why you see him and I, sometimes you see one of us down, one up. We understand. We understand this. This way.
See. And then he knows.
And we never let one another get out of step. See.
Yeah, I'll give him that whole time. Yeah.
Hold on to this last time.
Only this last time he messed me up. One, one, one. One time I done that.

This last time, I know he messed me up, baby. One, one, one time I done that. He kept saying to me, he said, Al, Al, Al. I said, I done. I said, every time I come, I come on. I said, no, I see them trucks. I said, son, I said, eat you, eat you. He said, you know something? He said, I done made the humbug. I said, I know you made the humbug. He said, I know you made the humbug. Yeah, that's right. You see, when I'm wrong, I'll give up. You understand? That's one thing to me. I don't care how good you can be wrong one time.
I don't care how good you can be wrong. I said, well, I said, it's me. I said, it's all me this time. And then the first time, since we've been playing the dead, I haven't gone on the line.

That was when we ended up around Claiborne and, what was it, Louisiana? Is that the one you're talking about? Where we rode back in the car together? Where you had the humbug? Yeah, we all came back in the car together.
Yeah, the thing. The left field? Yeah, that's the one. Yeah, yeah, the left field, yeah. The left field, yeah.
In the old days, I understand they used to march with the right foot on the first feet, like one, two, right, left.
But now they do it.

Now it's left. The army does the other way. Now the young fellows that went to the army, they do it the other way. But what do you all try to do now? Left. Left, right, left, right. Some of the other bands still, occasionally, see some of the old fellows put their first-
Yeah, the right, yeah, I understand.
Well I'm telling you, some of them don't know their right from their left. And I just don't know or care. They don't know right from their left.
And you see some's on the right, some's on the left, you see. And that is, it's all mixed up.

But listen, I can tell you one thing. This is a band of ours, the Yuriki band. You look at the picture, and I guarantee you, you would always see putting your, you know, the left foot in the eye, red and out, you got the same step. Because me, I watched them, you see, I keep them scared all the time. I take my horn, I hit them on the side. I say, what do you want to do?

You know, you know, you're right. You're right. You're right. You're right. You're right. You're right. You're right. You're right. You're right. You're right. And then the left foot in the eye, red and out, you got the same step. You see, my left foot is out there at all time. Because me, I watch them, you see them, I keep them scared all the time. I take my horn, I hit them on the side. I say, what's the step there? And then this time he changed and he gets on the step.

See, sometimes I turn around and look at a chick, you know. He says, watch it. Watch it. I say, I got it. I said, I got it, and I make my skip, and I got it. All I do is make that skip, and I get back in there.
When you started out, how did you do it?
With your step?
Left foot first or right foot?

Well, no, I tell you, they broke me in on that, you see. Well, they had to tell me, because I didn't know right from left, me. See, I didn't even know if you had to put the right foot down or the left foot, you see. Well, Clay Giles, he was one of them old-time drummers, ain't something? He was a bass drum beater. And so I told him, I said, Clay Giles, I said, I even don't know how to march. He said, that's all right. He says, come on, he says, come in my room. He said, now, listen, when I hit that drum, I said, now, put that left foot down. I put the left foot down. He said, now, every time I hit the drum, he said, you go. He said, put your left foot first, I hit. Now, you hit the right foot. He said, now your left foot. Now you hit the right foot. Clay Giles learned me out of march.
Well, now you say you played with his brother, huh? Were you the one who was saying that?
Yeah, I played with Clay Giles. He had a brother he called Oscar Giles.
Is that Albert Giles' uncle or father?
That's, Clay Giles is Albert's uncle.
I see.
That's his uncle. Now, his daddy was, let's see, I can't think of his daddy's name.
Well, we'll ask him. He'll know. Yeah. They'll know.
I can't think of his daddy. We'll get it. I just want to get those guys. I can't think of his daddy's name.

I was going to ask about, in marching, the trombones are always out in front, but where does the tuba belong? Right with you or sometimes the tuba in back of you in the old days? Way back. Well, the tuba...
The tuba supporters would always be in the front.

No, no, no, but some time ago the tuba used to be behind us, because if he had two trombones, then the tuba used to be back to the second. But now, here up late, we got to show that we go three in front.
Three in front.
Yeah.
But if you had only two in a row, then two trombones, then the tuba in back, who else back there with him?
Well, on this side, on that side, that's your tuba and your... Sex? Yeah.
Where'd the baritone horn go?
Alto, sex, and in the back, behind me.
Baritone horn back of you?
Yeah, behind me, yeah. Over on the right side? Yeah, behind that, yeah.
With the tuba? Yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Oh, yeah, you mean with the old thing?
Baritone.
That's right, with the tuba, that's right. Yeah, baritone. Where'd the alto horns come?
Yeah, he'd come next.
Next. Where was the clarinet?
Were they... They'd come next to the trumpet, but the trumpet would be last.
The trumpet's last, or the drums last?
The drums last. Yeah. The drums last. The drums last. Yeah. How come the Eureka does it the other way now? They put the trumpets in back?
Well, yeah. Is that Percy's idea?
I don't know how Poesies got that lined up now, but I noticed that myself. He put the drums in between Paul and then. Yeah. I noticed that myself.
In the old days, I understand the drums were always in back.
Always in back. Right.
I wonder if he had a reason for that, or...
I don't know. I don't know what was his reason or anything. I don't know.
I imagine he likes to stay back there where he can keep an eye on the whole band. I guess...
That might be it. Keep an eye on that time, you know? Yeah. So in case they get out of that time, well, then he could call them down.
That's the only band that does it that way that I ever saw. I wonder why you did it to them.

Yeah. That might be the reason. We'll ask Percy to... Yeah, you have to be... That might be his reason. You see, to keep... That when those drums get out of line, that he could be right there to... To guard them, you know? Mm-hmm. Get them in right.
See, I forgot to ask you why you were christened at.

I was christened at the oldest church in here. That's... St. Boniface. Catholic. Mm-hmm. And, well, that church now is not even in existence. Mm-hmm. It's, uh, it was back on, uh, Yalvis... Yalvis, Nonsagan. Oh, yeah.
Yeah.
And, uh...
Where did you go to school here? Roberson School.
The Robertson School. I first went to By Road School down at, uh... Durny and Governor Nicholas. Well, used to call it By Road Street then, back in those days. Mm-hmm. See?
Governor Nicholas was called By Road? Yeah.

Back in those days it was By Road Street, you see? Mm-hmm. Now they called it Governor Nicholas. Mm-hmm. But that was an old break building was there. Now they got a new school there, you see. You got a new school there. See, well, way back in that time they had all white teachers in there. Mm-hmm. Well, after they moved us from there, they moved us up to Bienville and Roberson, the old Roberson school across from the cemetery. These were public schools? Public schools, yeah. See, then from that school, and then that's where they tore this, tore the door of that school down there, they built up the one on Bienville Street, they called it the Wicker School. Wicker School, that's old Roberson School. Mm-hmm. See? That's way back in 19... 1910, so no further back than that. 1903. I wasn't here then. Yeah. Did you have a band at school? No, they didn't. They used to teach you music, but they didn't have any bands. They wasn't teaching you music in school. All they did was teach you the notes and things, you know. Would you sing or...? Had a great big, yeah, they used to learn you how to sing. They had a great big, oh, you know, like them great big sheets, you know. Mm-hmm. Oh, yeah. And they had notes and things on there, learn you different notes, and they'd throw that sheet over and get the next lesson if they had. It was just the same like, you know, like they used to have some of these Sunday schools, Sunday, like they have those lessons on, they'd throw them sheets over. Yeah, that's what it looks like, you see. That's the way they used to learn you how to read music. But they didn't have any teaching the bands or anything. Teaching the bands, that just come up here lately, taking the long yard to play music in these schools.
What did they have in the churches now? Did they have an organ in the church or a piano or any instrument or whatever?
Well, you mean way back in time, in the olden time? Yeah. Well, no, most of it was organs. They didn't have no pianos that I know of.
And what about out in the country?

Well, they didn't have no piano or nothing, your voice, you know. See back- Get out there and tough it up, you understand? With your voice, everybody would get together, understand, and sing together.

See, they used to call them melodions. They was a red thing and they had like pipes, you know, come up. They had small one and then they'd go right on straight on up. Some as long as what he is. They had like hole cut in them like them flutes. They used to call them melodions. And in the later years they started calling them organ, pipe organs. Well then they'd have a fellow back there, he'd be there pumping the thing while the organs be playing, you see. But he'd be back there, he had to be pumping that. See, as long as she's playing well, he just had to stay there and pump.
I used to do that thing.
You did it too? Well then you know what I'm talking about, eh? You know what I'm talking about, eh? What they call the melodions, eh?
Well, this is a pipe organ.
Pipe organ, right? Pipe organ, yeah. They had them big pipes there.
I didn't know you were a musician. Uh-uh. Huh? You didn't know he was a violin?

He was a musician. He was pumping his way through. Yeah. You know what I was talking about, eh? You just was listening, and you'd find out what I was talking about. That old fella used to be back there, man. He had that poor handle. Sometimes you see he'd be weak back there. You see him pumping there, but he kept pumping until it stopped.

I'm wondering about some more of the trombonists when you were young. Did you ever hear Roy Palmer? Do you remember Roy Palmer? No, I don't remember Roy Palmer. Played in the district a little. Who were some of the trombonists when you first started playing that you heard?

I heard, uh, this fella, a young fella, yeah, he was, oh, I can't think of that boy's name. He left, yeah, Zoo Robinson. I was gonna ask you, just start asking, yeah, Zoo Robinson. Zoo Robinson. Well, he was a good friend of ours, you know. He was a good musician. Mm-hmm. Zoo Robinson. Well, I heard this other boy, this boy.
Lord Dutre.
Dutre.
He was a good one, too.
And, uh...
George Fields was a good one, too. George Fields. Uh, let me see. And another boy, uh... Akin used to play, too. Akin. I saw his grave.
This other, whatchacob, Ned, is, uh, Vig Gasper? Oh, yeah, Vig Gasper. Oh, yeah, yeah. Vig Gasper, yeah. Vig Gasper. Remember anybody named Baptiste? Oh, oh, oh, that, that... Baptiste.
Baptiste, yeah, yeah. Oh, man, that's some kind of...
He was a hero. I don't remember. You know what? I remember. You know what? Baptiste. Baptiste Delay, oh?
Yeah, Baptiste Delay, yeah. Baptiste Delay, yeah.
Baptiste Delay, yeah.
Oh, man. I know it don't belong well.
That's right. Baptiste Delay. I think he was the first one to start playing drumming, I think. That's when I heard, I don't know. Baptiste Delay, yeah.
First one to start playing drumming? Slide drumming. Slide. Slide. Yeah, Slide. Yeah, Baptiste Delay. He used to play all his halls around here. You're Morris French.
Yeah.
Well, Morris French, yeah. Well, Morris French, yeah. Morris French, he come after all those fellas. He was young. Yeah, he come after those fellas.
He was good too.
Yeah, he was all right. Yeah. Yeah, he's good. Garrido. Yeah, Morris French. This boy, what I was telling you about, said it left you in Winterweather.
Drew Robertson.
Drew Robertson. Drew Robertson.
Yeah. You remember him too, Sonny?
I played with him too, in the Allen Band a couple of times.
Was he, did he play Barrow House too, or did he just read?

Yeah, yeah, he could read and play Barrow House. Yeah, he was all around there. He played down the district there. He played down the district there. He played down the district some time before he left here. Then he went away and he came back and he played down that wall and he left and went on
off again. Well, I'm too young to know about the district. What was that? I mean, like, what was it?
Well, that was when.
I never really got a good picture of that. Well, that was when you wanted to be loved up, you see, go down there. Would they have bands in the houses or?

They'd have bands in all them different ballrooms, like Tom Anderson's and Basin Street was in Bloom then, you see. You'd catch a band at this corner, band across the street, band around the corner, band on that side, most every corner you hit they had a band. You used to call them cabarets. See, like they got them now ballrooms and cafes and things, but back in that time they called them cabarets.
What was Zoo up to down there? I mean, who was he with?

Well, I don't know what particular band he was with, but he played at the lyrics a couple of times there with, what's that old man named, violin player? Robeshoe. Robeshoe. Yeah, Robeshoe. Yeah. Zoo played with Robeshoe a while at the old lyrics.
I played that too, about four or five times already. It was a John Robeshoe old band. John Robeshoe, yeah.
Well, what kind of bands would they have in the district? Would they have musical bands or would they need barrel house?

They'd have mostly string instruments, sometimes trumpets in between there. Sometimes they'd have a bass, mandolin, guitar. Sometimes they'd have a full band, but at that time they had six piece bands, you see. They'd have trombone, cornet, clarinet, bass, drum, and banjo. They mostly would use banjos back in those days, you see.
Would the string trios like that, when they have three pieces, would they play in one place or would they wander around from one place to another?

They'd play in one place. You see, now like, say like if Tom Anderson had them. You see, they'd stay there and Tom Anderson would play. Then they had others that would, used to call hustlers. Well, they'd play at this place a while and they'd go down there and there. Oh, well. You see. But like Tom Anderson, Tom Anderson had his regular men's.
Was that being Nookie Johnson? Did you know him?
Johnson.
And Willie Jackson. Willie Jackson. Nookie Johnson and Willie Jackson. Two singers.

That old man used to play bass, I can't think of his name. Just died recently? Oh no, he'd been dead. He was a bass player. Well him and Johnson and this other fellow that he was talking about, there's three of them used to play together. One played the mandle, one played the guitar and the other played the bass. But there was the one composed that song about Maestress Wagner and Vinny on taking my furniture and gone.
I don't know that. How does that go say?

See, there was a song there. They had a furniture store there on Ramport where, Ramport in Iberville. See, that fellow would come to you to collect on his furniture. You didn't have money to pay. Well then, you know, you need to have the wagon back up there to take your furniture. So, he taking so many people's furniture away from them until these dudes just composed a song. So they said, Maestress Wagner and Vinny on and take my furniture and gone away. They just composed. I can't think of the whole thing, you know. But that's the way they're there. You remember that? Yeah, I remember that. Yeah, because they were still singing when you was back sitting in school.
Yeah, Maestress Wagner and Vinny took my furniture and gone away. Maestress Wagner and Vinny took my furniture and gone. Maestress Wagner and Vinny took my furniture and gone.
Maestress Wagner and Vinny took my furniture and gone. They were all, they were, them three fellows that weren't composed that song.
This guy's been dead, huh?
Oh, yeah.
Well, that, this is thoughts of guessing, Gabe. Johnny Prudence?
Johnny Prudence. Johnny Prudence used to play with me in the Camellia band.
Yeah. It wasn't him, huh?
No.
What was that guy? The living days from across the river.
This fella was, no he stayed on this side, he stayed right around up in this district part. He was a big tall fella. Brown? No, his name ain't Brown.

French name, like a French fella? I'm trying to think of that dude's name. Roman Breaux used to play in the trio, mandolin with the Bunch too. Yeah. I can't think of that dude's name. Somebody from Glenny's era, around the time of Glenny, huh? Way around the time of Albert Glenny. We'll check into it. Yeah, we'll find somebody else. He'll mention it again sometime.
He used to play at Tom Anderson's. His daddy used to shine shoes around up in there. Daddy used to shine shoes and used to play bass.
Did you know Bob Lyons, by the way?
Oh yeah, Bob Lyons, yeah.
What kind of musician was he? Hell.

He was a routineer too, wasn't he? Hell. He was a routineer, yeah. He was a routineer. Yeah, a ham. He was a ham. He was a big ham too. Yeah, a routineer. Yeah, a routineer. He was a routineer, sister. But I tell you. Most everything that came from around Ramport and Bedee, the round of the neighborhood, that was mostly. Ham. We used to call them jambon. In French that mean ham. Jambon. Jambon. Jambon.
You speak French, Tim. I don't know. I don't know. I call them ham. Well, that's all the same. Ham right on. See?
Oh, down in the country, Sonny, do you remember any guitars or banjos down that way?

Well, I'm going to tell you no, they didn't have no banjos down there, no guitars at that time. All they know is to blow and beat. Beat you with and blow your way out. And I was in the bunch to blow your way out. Trombone, bass, and baritone. I can play that. Because what's the difference is it's the same clip. I know the trumpet, I used to play the trumpet, now what's the difference in the trumpet and the baritone? It's the same doggone finger.
Do you use the same mouthpiece on trombone and baritone? Yes, of course.
Yeah, you can use the same mouthpiece.
Same thing.

The baritone mouthpiece might be a little smaller, but you still can use yours. You see like the one I used? You can use that on the baritone. That's the same size. The baritone, they fish the same size. It's the same thing.
Did you ever play anything else?
I started to learn baritone, but I give it up.
Tuba, carnet, you never tried it? No, I never tried it.
I had that around the house and I never did work with it.
How come you didn't like baritone?

I don't know myself. It's a sweet instrument, that is. I picked it up, they gave it to me up at the office too. Yeah, the fellow gave me baritone up at the office and I had it home there. And I fooled around and sold the thing. You see I was so busy, I had so much on my hand. I had my wife then, seven kids, and I had my pressing business to run. I was waking up in the office.
